newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers in Oklahoma City bomb case end arguments.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers in Oklahoma City bomb case end arguments.

text.p: The evidence against each of the defendants in the Oklahoma City bombing case contrasts so sharply it would be unfair to try the two men together, a defence lawyer argued in a pre-trial hearing on Thursday.

Defendants Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols, charged in the April 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that claimed the lives of 168 people, were seeking to have their trials separated.
On Wednesday experts testified on the severance motion and on Thursday lawyers concluded their arguments.
In another matter in the pre-trial hearing, U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch ordered prosecutors to respond to 56 requests from McVeigh's attorneys for information.

The McVeigh defence team is seeking national intelligence information that might support McVeigh's defence theory that the bombing was "inspired and financed by foreign terrorist organisations." But McVeigh's attorney Stephen Jones told the court he had no hard evidence at this point. "It may turn out to be nothing," he said.
Jones said he believes a coverup is going on, making it impossible for the defence to receive information on possible international links. Prosecutors denied this charge.
In the issue involving severing the two cases, Sean Connelly said the two defendants should be tried together because 95 percent of the evidence applied to both defendants.
Matsch was expected to rule on the defence motion for severance in several weeks. The hearing concludes on Friday.
The date for the actual trial was not set but was expected to begin in the first half of 1997.
Nichols' attorney Michael Tigar said his defendant was at home in Kansas on the day of the bombing, not in Oklahoma.

"On the morning of April 19, 1995, somebody got out of a (rental) truck and ignited a fuse. Whoever that was could see the people in that building and see them going in and out," Tigar told the court. He said that person would be in a very different situation than his defendant.

McVeigh's attorneys were concerned about statements Nichols made two days after the bombing when he spoke for 9-1/2 hours with local police in Herington, Kansas, and mentioned McVeigh's name at least 60 times.
The statements could only be used as evidence against Nichols, but defence attorneys argued it would be too much to ask of jurors to ignore the references to McVeigh.
Victims and their relatives want a single trial that will result in obtaining "justice much quicker," said Paul Heath, who was in the federal building at the time of the bombing.

McVeigh's lawyer Jones said he believed that if two trials were ordered the second would have to be three or four months after the conclusion of the first and might need to be held in a different city.
The trial was moved to Denver from Oklahoma because it was deemed impossible for the two defendants to receive a fair hearing in Oklahoma.
